<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7895, the PBM Kickback Prohibition Act, amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act\1\ (ERISA) to prohibit pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) from paying referral fees to brokers, consultants, and similar entities. In doing so, the legislation takes a modest step to address inappropriate compensation arrangements and potential conflicts of interest between brokers and consultants and PBMs that raise costs for both workers and employers alike. In previous congresses, the Committee on Education and Workforce (Committee) worked in a bipartisan manner to develop meaningful legislation that addresses related challenges that employer-sponsored health plans confront when working with PBMs. However, rather than engage in such a process in developing and advancing H.R. 7895, the Majority chose to proceed through a rushed, partisan approach that dismisses Democratic suggestions for improvements to this legislation. As a result, both the introduced and reported versions of H.R. 7895 are inadequate to address the scope of the problem the bill seeks to address. Instead, the bill serves primarily as a partisan talking point to promote President Trump's so-called ``Great Healthcare Plan.''\2\ Committee Democrats supported the legislation because it is a small step toward addressing misaligned incentives in health care. However, moving forward, the legislation should be improved to ensure that it meaningfully addresses the full scope of conflicts of interest among health plan service providers such as insurance companies, third party administrators, and other middlemen.
\1\Pub. L. No. 93-406 (1974).
\2\The Great Healthcare Plan, The White House (Jan. 2026), https:// www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/The-Great-Healthcare- Plan.pdf.
RISING COSTS INCREASINGLY MAKE HEALTH CARE UNAFFORDABLE FOR CONSUMERS
High health care costs represent an urgent issue for American consumers, who increasingly face unaffordable health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs. In 2024, total national health expenditures in the United States reached $5.3 trillion or 18.0 percent of gross domestic product.\3\ Americans' per capita health care spending has risen to $14,775, approximately double the average amount spent per capita in peer countries.\4\ These expenditures are heavily driven by high prescription drug prices and the rates charged by hospitals, physicians, and other providers.\5\ Additionally, growing health care spending is also directly correlated with rising administrative costs associated with middlemen, particularly for individuals with private health coverage.\6\
\3\Ctrs. for Medicare & Medicaid Servs., National Health Expenditures 2024 Highlights 1 (2026), https://www.cms.gov/files/ document/highlights.pdf.
\4\Imani Telesford et al., How Does Health Spending in the U.S. Compare to Other Countries?, Peterson-KFF Health Sys. Tracker (Mar. 11, 2026), https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/health-spending-u-s-compare-countries/.
\5\See Cong. Budget Off., The Prices That Commercial Health Insurers and Medicare Pay for Hospitals' and Physicians' Services (Jan. 2022), https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57778.
\6\See Linda J. Blumberg et al., Untangling the Complex Web: Summary of a New Expert Perspective, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Nov. 19, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/untangling-the-complex-web-summary-of-a-new-expert-perspective/.
Approximately 181 million people in the United States receive health coverage through an employment-based plan.\7\ Although individuals with job-based health benefits generally express satisfaction with their plans,\8\ rising health care costs present a substantial affordability challenge for millions of workers and their families. Since 2015, the average annual premium in an employer-sponsored family plan has risen 53 percent, reaching $26,993 in 2025.\9\ The average general annual deductible for single coverage in the employer market has increased 42.9 percent over the last decade, growing from $1,320 in 2015 to $1,886 in 2025.\10\ These rising costs continue to squeeze workers and their families, and addressing the drivers of these costs should be a top priority for Congress.
\7\Lisa N. Bunch & Halelujha Ketema, Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2024 2 (Sept. 2025), https://www2.census.gov/ library/publications/2025/demo/p60-288.pdf.
\8\What Leads to Greater Satisfaction With Health Plan Coverage?, Emp. Benefits Rsch. Inst. 1 (Apr. 6, 2023), https://www.ebri.org/docs/ default-source/fast-facts/ff-463-cehcs7-6 apr23.pdf?sfvrsn=c599392f_2.
\9\2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey 35, KFF (Oct. 22, 2025), https://files.kff.org/ attachment/Employer-Health-Benefits-Survey-2025-Annual-Survey.pdf.
\10\Id. at 101.
HEALTH PLAN SERVICE PROVIDERS OFTEN HAVE CONFLICTS OF INTEREST THAT
HARM CONSUMERS
Employers who sponsor health plans often rely on a range of service providers to assist in administering and managing their plans. While many such service providers play a valuable role in delivering benefits, their business models have also been described as ``a complex web of common ownership, contracting arrangements, and financial deals which create an array of conflicts of interests and hidden flows of money.''\11\ These business models can have an inflationary effect on health care spending, ultimately at the expense of consumers who must shoulder rising premiums and cost-sharing.\12\
\11\Blumberg et al., supra note 6.
\12\Id.
PBMs, which are the primary focus of H.R. 7895, are one such type of service provider. They contract with health plans to perform a number of services related to the administration of prescription drug benefits, including developing and maintaining lists of covered drugs (formularies), negotiating prices and rebates with drug manufacturers, and reimbursing pharmacies for drugs dispensed to plan participants.\13\ The opaqueness of PBM practices has received substantial scrutiny in recent years, resulting in major legislative reforms enacted by Congress in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026\14\ and a proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Labor earlier this year.\15\
\13\Christopher J. Sroka, Pharmacy Benefit Managers, Cong. Rsch. Serv. (Nov. 29, 2000), https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/ 20001129_RL30754_ae8115ed5c22ac5d657bb297e78f9a 8b62bd060f.pdf.
\14\Pub. L. No. 119-75, div. J, tit. VII (2026).
\15\Improving Transparency Into Pharmacy Benefit Manager Fee Disclosure, 91 Fed. Reg. 4,348 (Jan. 30, 2026), https:// www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-30/pdf/2026-01907.pdf.
However, PBMs are just one component of the ``complex web'' of middlemen whose business models harm consumers and employers alike. For example, the majority of workers with job-based health benefits are covered through a self-insured plan, in which the employer bears the financial risk, rather than an insurer.\16\ Due to the complexity of administering such plans, employers generally contract with third party administrators (TPAs) to perform critical functions with respect to the plans.\17\ These TPAs are often owned by commercial insurers that, in turn, often own hospitals and physician groups, creating structural conflicts of interest that misalign incentives to the detriment of both plan sponsors and workers.\18\
\16\Christine Monahan, Questionable Conduct: Allegations Against Insurers Acting as Third-Party Administrators, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Mar. 24, 2023), https://chir.georgetown.edu/ questionable-conduct-allegations-insurers-acting-third-party-administrators/.
\17\Karen Handorf et al., Third-Party Administrators--The Middlemen of Self-Funded Health Insurance, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (May 28, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/third-party-administrators-the-middlemen-of-self-funded-health-insurance/.
\18\Id.
Payments from these service providers to brokers and consultants are one such example of potential conflict of interest. A 2023 article in Stat investigated the fees paid by PBMs to certain brokers and consultants who encouraged their clients to contract with PBMs from whom they received such payments.\19\ However, this article highlights just one instance of such fees steering plans toward favored service providers. In 2019, for example, ProPublica found that insurers frequently pay commissions to brokers based on the number of employers they enroll in coverage.\20\ These fees are substantial, often between three to six percent of the plans' premiums, creating an incentive to further drive up health care spending.\21\ Similar compensation arrangements, regardless of whether the payments are made by PBMs or any other service provider, steer health plans toward service providers who generate profits for brokers and consultants but may not be the best choice for employers and workers.
\19\Bob Herman, It's Beyond unethical' Opaque Conflicts of Interest Permeate Prescription Drug Benefits, Stat (June 23, 2023), https:// www.statnews.com/2023/06/20/pbms-consulting-firms-investigation/.
\20\Marshall Allen, Behind the Scenes, Health Insurers Use Cash and Gifts to Sway Which Benefits Employers Choose, ProPublica (Feb. 20, 2019), https://www.propublica.org/article/health-insurance-brokers-cost-commissions-bonuses.
\21\Id.
THE COMMITTEE HAS PREVIOUSLY WORKED IN A BIPARTISAN MANNER TO IMPROVE
TRANSPARENCY
The Committee has a long history of working in a bipartisan manner to address problems in employer-sponsored health plans. These efforts have resulted in meaningful reforms that increase transparency and have protected consumers from the rising costs of health care.
During the 116th Congress, the Committee negotiated and advanced H.R. 5800, the Ban Surprise Billing Act,\22\ introduced by Rep. Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott (D-VA) and Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC). This legislation addressed the pernicious issue of surprise medical billing by out-of-network health care providers and relied on a benchmark payment rate that would help keep prices down. Additionally, it shined a light on excessive fees and conflicts of interest among service providers such as brokers, consultants, PBMs, and TPAs by requiring disclosure of direct and indirect compensation to plan fiduciaries. Several provisions of the ConsolidatedAppropriations Act, 2021 (CAA 2021)\23\ incorporated the Committee's efforts, including groundbreaking service provider disclosure requirements added to section 408(b)(2) of ERISA.\24\
\23\See Pub. L. No. 116-260, div. BB (2020).
\24\See 29 U.S.C. Sec. 1108(b)(2)(B).
\22\H. Rept. No. 116-615 at 49 (2020).
In the 118th Congress, the Committee took a number of additional actions to reduce costs and address conflicts of interest, including the markup of a package of bills relating to transparency. These bills included H.R. 2401, the Hidden Fee Disclosure Act, introduced by Rep. Joe Courtney (D-CT) and Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN), which strengthened the 408(b)(2) disclosure requirements to ensure that plan fiduciaries have information needed to responsibly monitor TPAs and PBMs for conflicts of interest. Additionally, H.R. 4507, the Transparency in Coverage Act, introduced by Rep. Bob Good (R- VA) and Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA), improved transparency by, among other reforms, requiring PBMs to disclose their rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration. This bipartisan work contributed to the enactment of similar reforms in the 119th Congress as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA 2026),\25\ including similar PBM reporting requirements and a clarification of which service providers must fully disclose their direct and indirect compensation under section 408(b)(2).\26\
\25\Pub. L. No. 119-75 (2026).
\26\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1108(b)(2)(B)(ii)(bb).
